edition.deck: A claimed Ukraine energy truce meets fresh attacks and unanswered questions, as pressure builds on governments over security, public services and household costs.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritise consequential developments while distinguishing confirmed events from claims and analysis. The Ukraine ceasefire remains unconfirmed by Moscow; reporting on the Danish data breach and suspected drone sightings also leaves important questions unanswered.

content.headline: Trump claims Russia and Ukraine agreed to an energy ceasefire, but details are M
content.shortHeadline: Trump claims energy truce; Russia has yet to confirm
content.standfirst: Volodymyr Zelensky says Ukraine is ready to stop attacks on Russian energy sites if Moscow does the same. The claim comes amid continuing strikes and a dispute over US plans to ease sanctions on Russian diesel.

image.caption: Cars burn after a Russian strike in Kharkiv, where a power plant was also hit.

sources.originalTitle: Trump announces partial ceasefire in Ukraine war as Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’
Trump's 'energy ceasefire' claim welcomed by Zelensky but Russia silent
Ukraine kender ikke detaljer i mulig energi-våbenhvile
Ukraine war briefing: Russia attacks multiple power plants after Trump energy ceasefire claim
Putin sees Trump as the gift that keeps on giving

segments.body: Donald Trump said Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate ceasefire on attacks against energy infrastructure, but gave no details. Zelensky said the announcement was news to him; Kyiv would accept a reciprocal truce, but Russia had not confirmed it.

segments.title: Attacks and pressure
segments.body: Ukraine said Russian drones struck energy sites, including a power plant in Kyiv and one in Kharkiv, and officials reported six people killed in attacks on two Ukrainian cities. The claim follows Trump’s announcement of a deal to import Russian diesel while temporarily easing sanctions—a move Zelensky and other allies say could help finance Moscow’s war.

The Guardian’s analysis argues that the diesel agreement is a political win for Vladimir Putin even if promised shipments do not materialise. That is analysis, not a confirmed outcome; the scale and effect of any fuel exports remain uncertain.

perspectives.body: The i Paper’s Mark Galeotti argues the agreement benefits Putin diplomatically even before any diesel is shipped, while questioning whether Russia can deliver the promised volumes.

content.headline: Houthi attacks hit Riyadh airport again as Saudi Arabia weighs its response
content.shortHeadline: Fresh Houthi strike on Riyadh airport kills one
content.standfirst: A second attack on King Khalid International Airport in two days killed one person and injured 11, Saudi authorities said. The escalation raises the risk of wider involvement in Yemen as the US considers its next move.

image.caption: Dust and debris inside King Khalid International Airport after an attack.

sources.originalTitle: Riyadh airport hit again after deadly Houthi missile attack, Saudi authorities say
One killed, 11 injured in second Houthi strike on Riyadh airport in two days
Én dræbt og 11 såret i nyt angreb på lufthavn i Saudi-Arabien
Riyadh airport attacks another dangerous moment in already tense conflict

segments.body: An unidentified projectile hit a passenger terminal at Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on Sunday, starting a fire and killing one person, Saudi civil aviation authorities said. Eleven people were injured. The Houthis claimed responsibility for attacks on the airport; Saudi air defences said they intercepted a cruise missile nearby.

segments.title: Wider regional risks
segments.body: The latest attack came a day after a strike at the airport killed 13 people and injured more than 300, according to the Guardian. The Houthis have warned airlines and passengers away from Saudi airports. The US has provided intelligence support, while President Trump has said he is considering whether to intervene militarily.

perspectives.body: The BBC analysis says the attacks threaten Saudi Arabia’s reputation for stability and could put pressure on Washington to respond, while warning that any military escalation may deepen an already complex conflict.

segments.body: The Houthis said Saudi strikes hit a home in Sana’a, killing a child and injuring six, but the BBC could not verify that report. The extent of damage at Dammam airport was also still being assessed, according to Saudi authorities.

content.headline: At least 139 migrants dead after boat capsizes off Djibouti, UN agency says
content.shortHeadline: At least 139 migrants dead in Djibouti boat disaster
content.standfirst: The boat was carrying 305 people from Djibouti to Yemen when it capsized near Obock. The International Organization for Migration revised its death toll after more bodies were recovered; others remain missing.

image.caption: IOM workers receive migrants near the port town of Obock.

sources.originalTitle: Children among 139 dead after boat capsizes off Djibouti, UN says

segments.body: At least 139 people, including 15 children, died after a boat carrying 305 migrants capsized off Djibouti on Thursday night, the International Organization for Migration said. About 82 people were rescued, and dozens were still missing. The agency revised its toll from 109 after 30 more bodies were recovered.

segments.title: A perilous route
segments.body: The survivors are Ethiopian nationals, and the IOM is assisting some of them in Obock. Tens of thousands of people make the dangerous journey from the Horn of Africa towards Yemen each year, seeking safety and work despite the conflict there. More than 900 people died or went missing on the route in 2025, according to the agency.

content.headline: Myanmar junta conscription drives bring fear of abduction and forced service
content.shortHeadline: Young people in Myanmar fear forced recruitment
content.standfirst: Residents describe young people being seized from streets and workplaces as the military struggles to meet recruitment quotas. Reporting documents allegations of coercion and payments, while authorities declined to comment on the cases.

image.caption: Authorities have reportedly ordered officials to meet military recruitment quotas in Myanmar.

sources.originalTitle: Young men live in fear of being snatched off the streets and sold to Myanmar's army

segments.body: Young men in Hpa-An, in Myanmar’s Karen state, say they fear being taken for military service. The BBC reports that residents describe plain-clothed junta supporters arresting people in their teens, twenties and thirties; some families tell young people to be home before dark.

segments.title: Pressure to fill the ranks
segments.body: A mandatory conscription law introduced in 2024 requires men aged 18 to 35 and women aged 18 to 27 to serve. Leaked documents seen by the BBC reportedly direct officials to meet recruitment quotas. A former military officer and other observers describe abductions, extortion and forced recruitment; the government’s recruitment body declined to comment to the BBC.

One woman told the BBC that her husband was taken after a relative allegedly transferred him to another ward to meet its quota. The official involved denied that money changed hands. The BBC could not reach the relative, and the woman says she still does not know where her husband is.

content.headline: Rights group says air strikes killed 72 gold prospectors on Sudan-Egypt border
content.shortHeadline: Rights group reports 72 dead in Sudan border strikes
content.standfirst: Emergency Lawyers says civilians prospecting for gold were killed in strikes in Sudan’s River Nile state. Neither Egypt nor Sudan’s de facto authorities had commented, and the group said its provisional death toll could rise.

image.caption: File photograph of gold prospectors in northern Sudan.

sources.originalTitle: Dozens of gold prospectors killed in strikes on Egypt-Sudan border, rights group says
72 personer dræbt ved guldmine, siger ngo

segments.body: At least 72 civilians were killed in air strikes on a gold-prospecting camp in Sudan’s River Nile state, the rights group Emergency Lawyers said. It said the toll was provisional. Egypt and Sudan’s de facto authorities had not commented on the reported attack.

segments.title: A contested border
segments.body: A survivor cited by Sudan Tribune, as reported by the BBC, said many more people were injured and described missiles hitting camps and excavation pits. The account and a higher possible toll have not been independently confirmed. The area has seen earlier allegations of Egyptian strikes on artisanal mining sites, which Cairo has not commented on in this report.

Artisanal gold mining has expanded during Sudan’s civil war, including in remote border areas where smuggling is a concern. The competing pressures around gold and border security add context, but do not establish who carried out Saturday’s reported strikes.

content.headline: Polish PM links school attacks to online violence as police make 117 arrests
content.shortHeadline: Poland investigates school attacks and online threats
content.standfirst: Three attacks at Polish schools this week left a caretaker dead and others injured, including children. Police arrested 117 people over weapons or threats as authorities investigated what the prime minister called a rise in online glorification of violence.

image.caption: A caretaker was killed at a primary school north of Warsaw this week.

sources.originalTitle: Poland stabbings driven by online glorification of violence, Tusk says

segments.body: Three violent incidents at Polish schools this week left a caretaker dead and others injured, including children, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said. Police arrested 117 people across the country for possessing weapons or threatening attacks after searching tens of thousands of schools.

segments.title: What authorities say
segments.body: Tusk described the attacks as spontaneous actions inspired by online activity and associated them with nihilistic violence and the extreme right. Police said they had not found evidence of a large organised group. The incidents prompted a nationwide police presence at schools and rumours of further attacks.

content.headline: Microsoft president urges binding AI safety rules as UK weighs its role
content.shortHeadline: Microsoft’s Smith calls for enforceable AI safety rules
content.standfirst: Brad Smith says AI needs safety obligations including incident reporting and emergency brakes, putting him at odds with Donald Trump’s preference for industry self-regulation. UK ministers are also under pressure to strengthen safeguards and cyber defences.

image.caption: Liquid-cooled servers at a London data centre.

sources.originalTitle: AI is less regulated than milk, says Microsoft president
UK to strengthen cyber defences as minister calls for AI firms to increase safety efforts

segments.body: Microsoft president Brad Smith called for global safety rules for AI, including a legal duty to report incidents and tell people when an AI system has gone wrong. He also proposed emergency mechanisms to pause systems and independent government evaluation before some products are released.

segments.title: Security concerns
segments.body: Former UK AI Security Institute chief scientist Geoffrey Irving warned the Guardian that companies may not be able to prevent an adversarial country stealing unreleased models. The report also described an OpenAI security test in which researchers said the potential scope of access was large; OpenAI says it has protections including encryption and monitoring.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s reporting adds a national-security dimension: Geoffrey Irving warns that model theft is a risk, while a UK minister is expected to argue that Britain cannot rely entirely on companies to police their own systems.

segments.body: Smith’s call for regulation contrasts with Trump’s stated preference for self-policing by US companies. Smith argued that responsible firms may follow voluntary rules, but legislation is needed to address companies that do not.

content.headline: US justice department investigates broadcasters over Trump pool coverage
content.shortHeadline: US investigates networks over Trump coverage boycott
content.standfirst: The Justice Department has asked five broadcasters for communications after they paused shared coverage in protest at White House restrictions on some reporters. The probe raises questions about competition law and press access.

image.caption: The dispute over the White House press pool disrupted live TV coverage of Trump events.

sources.originalTitle: US justice department investigates TV networks over Trump pool coverage
Amerikansk ministerium efterforsker tv-stationer efter boykot af Trump
Thin-skinned Trump still desperately wants our attention

segments.body: The US Justice Department is investigating ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News over whether their temporary suspension of shared coverage of Donald Trump breached federal competition law. The department requested communications relating to the broadcasters’ response to White House restrictions on reporters from CNN, MS Now and Politico.

segments.title: Press access and legal questions
segments.body: The White House restored the three outlets’ access after a judge’s ruling in their case challenging the restrictions. The Justice Department says its antitrust division is investigating whether the broadcasters violated the law; the networks had not commented in the reporting supplied.

perspectives.body: The i Paper’s commentary argues that the investigation could become another means of pressuring outlets over coverage of Trump. That is the writer’s interpretation; the legal investigation’s outcome is not known.

content.headline: Iran war price shock puts pressure on Healey’s first Budget, IFS warns
content.shortHeadline: IFS warns Iran war could squeeze first Budget
content.standfirst: Higher inflation and borrowing costs could force the chancellor to choose between spending cuts, tax rises or accepting tighter budgets, the Institute for Fiscal Studies says. Its forecasts are unusually uncertain, and the Budget is due on 28 October.

sources.originalTitle: Iran war threatens Healey's Budget plans, think tank warns
‘John is f**ked. There is nothing there’: Budget troubles mount for Healey

segments.body: The Iran war’s impact on energy prices and borrowing costs poses a major challenge for Chancellor John Healey’s first Budget, the Institute for Fiscal Studies says. It warns that inflation could erode departments’ spending plans, leaving the government to make difficult choices about services, taxes or future budgets.

segments.title: A narrower margin
segments.body: The IFS estimates that borrowing costs could be about £10bn higher in 2029-30 and that the government’s fiscal-rule buffer could shrink to around £20bn. It says maintaining departmental budgets against inflation could require an extra £25bn that year, before any increase in defence spending; the official forecast may differ.

The institute warns against balancing the Budget with future spending cuts the government does not intend to deliver. Its director says doing so would make the plan a “work of fiction”. The Treasury declined to comment on speculation, while Healey has said fiscal discipline will underpin his Budget.

content.headline: Burnham says Russia interfered in Brexit vote but gives no evidence
content.shortHeadline: Burnham says Russia interfered in 2016 Brexit vote
content.standfirst: The prime minister says he received a “clear answer” that Russia interfered in the referendum, but has not disclosed who provided the assessment or what it was based on. A parliamentary committee previously criticised the failure to investigate the issue fully.

image.caption: Andy Burnham says he received a clear answer that Russia interfered in the referendum.

sources.originalTitle: Andy Burnham says it is clear Russia interfered in Brexit referendum
PM says it is 'clear' Russia interfered with Brexit vote
Der var russisk indblanding i brexit, siger premierminister
Rusland blandede sig i brexit-afstemning, siger premierminister

segments.body: Andy Burnham said he asked on entering Downing Street whether Russia had interfered in the 2016 Brexit referendum and received the answer that it had. He did not identify who gave him that assessment, describe the evidence or say whether interference affected the result.

segments.title: What is on the record
segments.body: A 2020 parliamentary Intelligence and Security Committee report criticised the government for failing to seek a full assessment of possible Russian activity. It cited evidence of attempts to influence British politics through state-backed media and social media, but did not establish that Russia changed the referendum result.

Britain Unbound, a pro-Brexit campaign group, called Burnham’s remarks an attempt to undermine the 2016 decision and said there was no good reason to believe Russian intervention influenced the outcome. The supplied reporting gives no further detail on the prime minister’s new assessment.

content.headline: Probation failures left more than 5,000 offenders without required tags
content.shortHeadline: Report finds thousands of offenders went untagged
content.standfirst: A new Institute for Government report says more than 5,000 people subject to electronic monitoring were not tagged in the first four months of the year. It warns that staff shortages and unreliable devices undermine supervision and public confidence.

image.caption: The report says the electronic tagging system is failing to meet demand.

sources.originalTitle: Failure to fit tags left 5,000 offenders unmonitored in England and Wales, report finds

segments.body: More than 5,000 people who should have been monitored were not tagged between January and April, about 15% of those with electronic tagging orders, an Institute for Government report says. Nearly 1,600 tags also failed to send a signal for at least two weeks.

segments.title: Wider strain on probation
segments.body: The report, based on public data and staff interviews, says staff shortages have left probation supervision rationed and sentences less meaningful. None of the probation units inspected in 2024 or 2025 received a rating above “requires improvement”; two-thirds were rated “inadequate”.

The report warns that expanded early release and electronic monitoring could add to the workload of an already stretched service. It recommends steadily increasing probation staff and making sentences clearer about time in prison and supervised in the community. The government says it is investing in probation and expanding monitoring.

content.headline: Drought leaves Lundy short of water, with visitor limits and evacuation fears
content.shortHeadline: Lundy rations water after months without rain
content.standfirst: The island off Devon has gone without significant rain since May, leaving its water supply critically low. Residents have imposed restrictions and brought water by boat; a new tank is planned, but a sustainable long-term solution is still needed.

image.caption: Lundy manager Matt Scantlebury stands in shallow water at Pondsbury, one of the island’s freshwater pools.

sources.originalTitle: Rapid showers and no flushing toilets: drought pushes Lundy island to the brink

segments.body: Lundy, home to 28 people, is facing severe water shortages after receiving no significant rain since the start of May. Its tanks fell to 13% capacity, enough for about a week, and the island brought water over by boat. A freshwater pool temporarily helped, but was itself starting to run low.

segments.title: Living with restrictions
segments.body: The campsite closed, pub toilets were shut and visitors were asked to use less water. Residents describe taking shorter showers and reusing water to flush toilets. A new 300,000-litre tank has been ordered; desalination has been discussed, but the island manager says it could be costly and energy-intensive.

The island’s manager and residents link the crisis to hotter, drier summers and Lundy’s exposed geography. The report describes an immediate need to conserve water, but no final long-term solution; rain was not forecast in the near term at the time of reporting.

content.headline: Farmers warn rising costs and climate shocks threaten UK food security
content.shortHeadline: Farmers warn costs and climate risks threaten food supply
content.standfirst: Farm fuel and fertiliser costs have surged as growers prepare for the next crop, following a record-hot summer and poor cereals harvest. Farmers and food experts say the UK needs stronger plans for overlapping shocks to its supply chains.

image.caption: NFU crops board chair Jamie Burrows says farmers face mounting pressures.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Some aren’t going to make it’: how pressure on farmers threatens UK food security

segments.body: Farmers warn that higher costs are making it harder to finance the next crop. The National Farmers’ Union says red diesel has almost doubled in price since the Iran conflict began, while fertiliser and animal feed costs have risen about 20%. The warning follows England’s worst recorded cereals harvest after a hot, dry summer.

segments.title: Exposure to disruption
segments.body: The UK produces about 60% of the food it needs and relies on imports and a concentrated distribution network. The National Audit Office has identified shortcomings in government catastrophe planning, while more than 150 food experts and academics recently warned that ministers lack a plan for feeding people in an emergency.

Experts cited in the report point to climate change, water scarcity, geopolitical shocks, energy outages and cyber-attacks as risks that could overlap. Farmers and food businesses say longer-term contracts, resilient soils and better contingency planning could help; Parliament’s public accounts committee is beginning an inquiry into supply resilience.

content.headline: EU fee offer could cost UK universities £280m in Brexit reset talks
content.shortHeadline: EU tuition-fee offer could cost universities £280m
content.standfirst: A compromise to lower fees for EU students could still leave UK universities with a £280m shortfall, sector modelling suggests. The proposal is part of wider negotiations over student mobility and a Brexit reset, while Britain also seeks access to proposed EU industry rules.

image.caption: Electric cars are among the industries affected by the EU’s proposed “Made in Europe” rules.

sources.originalTitle: UK universities face £280m Brexit reset bill as EU demands cheaper student fees
The EU decision that could force Burnham into major Brexit reset trade-off
The new EV threat to UK Brexit deal

segments.body: The EU has reportedly offered a compromise on fees for European students, setting them closer to the cost of delivering a course than to domestic rates. Modelling based on current EU student numbers estimates the change could cost UK universities about £280m; the institutions warn of pressure on jobs, courses and places for UK students.

segments.title: A wider negotiating trade-off
segments.body: The fee question is tied to a proposed youth mobility deal and a wider Brexit reset. Britain is also seeking inclusion in the EU’s proposed “Made in Europe” industrial policy, which could favour European suppliers in public contracts and subsidies. EU countries remain divided over whether the UK should qualify, and no outcome is guaranteed.

The Russell Group has previously estimated that charging EU students home fees would cost more than £500m, while the newer £280m figure is based on the EU’s reported compromise. Universities say any reduction in international-fee income would add to existing financial pressures. Negotiations are aiming for a summit in November.

content.headline: Government review warns rising ADHD diagnoses may bring risk of overdiagnosis
content.shortHeadline: Review flags possible overdiagnosis as ADHD diagnoses rise
content.standfirst: A government-commissioned review says diagnoses among some children are nearing or exceeding estimates of how common ADHD is, but stresses that this alone does not prove overdiagnosis at scale. It points to long waits and the challenge of subjective assessments.

image.caption: ADHD diagnosis rates among young people have risen over the past decade.

sources.originalTitle: The four reasons why ADHD experts fear the UK is heading towards overdiagnosis

segments.body: A government-commissioned review says ADHD diagnoses among some children and young people are approaching or exceeding estimates of the condition’s prevalence, and continue to rise. The authors say the figures do not, by themselves, establish that overdiagnosis is happening at scale; private diagnoses and waiting lists are not included in the NHS rates.

segments.title: Why diagnosis is difficult
segments.body: The review points to several possible drivers, including greater awareness, changing definitions and subjective assessments that rely on reported behaviour rather than blood tests or scans. It also raises concerns that private assessment clinics could have incentives to rush diagnoses, and recommends regulating them like NHS services.

The report’s authors stress the need to distinguish overdiagnosis from people who remain undiagnosed or are misdiagnosed. One co-author called the findings a warning sign rather than a definitive conclusion; experts say the evidence and people’s access to appropriate assessment and support need careful consideration.

content.headline: Pharmacy closures leave more patients travelling for essential medicines
content.shortHeadline: Pharmacy closures widen gaps in access to medicines
content.standfirst: Fifty-one pharmacies in England closed between January and August, including 31 in areas receiving extra access funding, analysis found. Patient groups warn that some people now face long journeys for prescriptions and advice.

image.caption: More than 50 pharmacies have closed in England this year, according to the analysis.

sources.originalTitle: The worst places to live if you are ill – where trips to chemists take an hour

segments.body: Fifty-one high-street pharmacies in England closed between January and August, about two a week, according to NHS figures analysed by the National Pharmacy Association. Thirty-one had received extra government funding intended to maintain access in areas with few alternatives.

segments.title: Unequal access
segments.body: A closure in Long Rock, Cornwall, left some residents facing a 17-mile round trip and up to 80 minutes by public transport to reach another pharmacy. The NPA says closures can make it harder to collect prescriptions and obtain advice, particularly for people with limited mobility or no transport.

The NPA says pharmacy funding has fallen in real terms since 2016, while Community Pharmacy England estimates the sector still has a funding gap despite a £340m government uplift. The government says it is investing in services; the Department of Health and Social Care and NHS England had been contacted for comment.

content.headline: Data breach exposes 8.8 million Danish CPR numbers; access route remains unclear
content.shortHeadline: Danish data breach exposes 8.8 million CPR numbers
content.standfirst: A compromised company with access to the national register is at the centre of Denmark’s largest reported CPR-number leak. The period of data theft is known, but investigators have not identified a suspect or confirmed the precise route of access.

image.caption: DR’s graphic illustrates a password linked to the company’s data leak.

sources.originalTitle: Afsløring: Fynsk virksomhed er centrum for massivt CPR-databrud
Fra Jesu fødsel til CPR: Her er historien om personnummeret

segments.body: Almost 8.8 million CPR numbers and addresses were taken from Denmark’s central register in what DR describes as the country’s largest such leak. The breach involved a small software company on Funen with authorised access to the register; the National Special Crime Unit is investigating and no one has been charged.

segments.title: What is known—and unknown
segments.body: A notice to the Danish Data Protection Agency says the theft occurred between 10 and 20 September and access was blocked on 2 October, after an unusually large invoice raised concern. DR found that a password used by the company had appeared in another data leak, but could not establish that this was the route used in the attack.

The breach has revived debate over whether Denmark should replace the CPR system. An information-science professor told DR that changing it would be difficult because it is embedded across public services, but said the incident could prompt a major tightening of security. The alleged hacker’s identity and motive remain unknown.

content.headline: TV 2 finds passenger flights were aloft during Danish army’s drone shootings
content.shortHeadline: Passenger planes were aloft during two drone shootings
content.standfirst: Flight data show passenger aircraft were in the air near a military range when soldiers fired at suspected drones on two occasions in 2025. Former pilots say misidentification is possible; the military maintains it fired at drones.

image.caption: Army commander Peter Boysen presents the account of the suspected drone shootings.

source.credit: Foto: Martin Sylvest / Ritzau Scanpix / TV 2

sources.originalTitle: Data afslører nyt sammenfald: To gange var passagerfly i luften under skud mod droner

segments.body: TV 2’s analysis of flight data found passenger aircraft in the air near the Borris military camp when soldiers fired at suspected drones on 25 and 28 September 2025. The outlet says the aircraft on 25 September passed through the area where the army commander said shots were fired, but the precise time of the shooting has not been provided.

segments.title: Different assessments
segments.body: Two former fighter pilots told TV 2 that lights from aircraft could have been mistaken for drones in the dark, when judging distance is difficult. The military maintains that soldiers fired at drones and says the passenger plane was too high to be relevant. The available reporting does not establish what the soldiers saw.

The newly reported 25 September shooting involved nine rounds fired at long range, according to the army commander’s account. TV 2 says the military has declined to give a more precise time or say whether it examined the possibility of confusion with aircraft.

content.headline: District heating bills set to rise as energy costs and grid limits bite
content.shortHeadline: District heating prices set to rise in several Danish towns
content.standfirst: Several district-heating companies have announced price rises for next year, including a 40% increase in Præstø. The company says limited access to electricity has forced it back to gas, while the industry warns prices may rise more widely.

image.caption: Several Danish district-heating companies have announced price increases for next year.

sources.originalTitle: Kæmpe stigninger i fjernvarmepriserne rammer

segments.body: District-heating prices are set to rise in several Danish towns. TV 2 reports increases of 40% in Præstø, 32% in Sønder Felding and 18% in Svendborg. Præstø resident Kenneth Hansen says his family will need to find an extra 650 kroner a month.

segments.title: Energy and network constraints
segments.body: Præstø Fjernvarme says it has returned to gas after being disconnected from the electricity grid 67 times because of overload. The company says it may wait up to 48 months for a permanent grid connection. Its chair says the lack of electricity has undermined the economics of its move away from fossil fuels.

The industry says heating costs depend on each company’s mix of gas, biomass, solar and electricity, and that price rises cannot be ruled out more broadly. The government has proposed funding for electrification and adopted an emergency plan for grid capacity, but the effect on future household bills remains uncertain.

content.headline: Denmark proposes 200-kroner fee for cruise passengers who come ashore
content.shortHeadline: Denmark proposes 200-kroner cruise passenger charge
content.standfirst: The government wants cruise passengers to pay 200 kroner when they come ashore from 2028, saying the levy would help address pollution, noise and congestion. Tourism and business groups warn it could deter visitors; the proposal is not yet law.

image.caption: The cruise ship MSC Euribia is docked at Copenhagen’s Nordhavn.

sources.originalTitle: Et enormt beløb eller en kop kaffe mindre: Regeringens forslag om krydstogtafgift splitter passagererne

segments.body: A proposed Danish budget measure would charge cruise passengers 200 kroner each time they come ashore, starting in 2028. The government expects the levy to raise 300 million kroner a year as cruise traffic grows, and says it would help cover pollution, congestion and noise.

segments.title: Tourism trade-off
segments.body: Business groups, Aarhus port and VisitAarhus fear the fee could make destinations less attractive and cost cities tourism income. Some passengers interviewed by DR said 200 kroner would not change their plans; others said the cost might persuade them to skip Denmark.
The proposal remains part of budget negotiations, which were expected to continue until December. The final charge, its design and its effect on cruise visits are not settled.

content.headline: Nuuk opens cancer advice centre as Greenland faces higher death rate
content.shortHeadline: Greenland opens cancer centre amid high death rate
content.standfirst: People in Greenland are about as likely to develop cancer as people in Denmark, but nearly twice as likely to die from it, according to a report. Late diagnosis and smoking are identified as factors; a new Nuuk centre will offer advice to patients and families.

image.caption: The new centre in Nuuk offers advice and support to people affected by cancer.

sources.originalTitle: Grønland åbner kræftrådgivningshus: Grønlændere har stadig langt større risiko for at dø af cancer end de nordiske naboer

segments.body: Greenland has a similar likelihood of cancer diagnoses to Denmark but nearly twice the risk of dying from the disease, according to a report cited at the opening of a cancer advice centre in Nuuk. Around 250 people in Greenland receive a cancer diagnosis each year.

segments.title: Access to support
segments.body: The report identifies late diagnosis and smoking as two factors in the higher death rate. The new centre, established by Greenland’s cancer association Neriuffiit Kattuffiat and the Danish Cancer Society, will advise patients and families during and after treatment.

People involved in the centre’s opening described the difficulties of seeking advice and medical attention across a vast territory where travel can be affected by weather. The reporting does not quantify how much the new service will change diagnosis or survival rates.

content.headline: Fallen tree disrupts trains across Funen as replacement buses are sent
content.shortHeadline: Fallen tree blocks trains across Funen
content.standfirst: A tree fell across both tracks between Aarup and Gelsted early on Monday, stopping trains between Odense and Fredericia. DSB ordered 30 replacement buses; its early-morning estimate was that rail services would not resume before 06:00.

sources.originalTitle: Væltet træ stopper alle tog over Vestfyn: 30 togbusser er på vej

segments.body: A fallen tree blocked both tracks between Aarup and Gelsted on Funen early on Monday, stopping trains between Odense and Fredericia. Intercity services between Zealand, Funen and Jutland were affected, DSB said.

DSB ordered 30 replacement buses. The first bus left Odense at 04:50; the operator said it had no firm forecast for restoring train services and did not expect trains to run across western Funen before 06:00. Passengers delayed by more than 30 minutes could use DSB’s travel guarantee.

content.headline: Manchester City beat Liverpool 3-0 at Anfield as financial case looms
content.shortHeadline: City beat Liverpool 3-0 amid financial-case uncertainty
content.standfirst: Erling Haaland, Jeremy Doku and Rayan Cherki scored in a commanding City win, their first match since an independent commission found the club had breached financial rules. City have appealed, and sanctions are yet to be announced.

image.caption: Liverpool fans display their opposition to Manchester City at Anfield.

sources.originalTitle: Man City's statement win has feeling of irrelevance with season in limbo
Manchester City
Winless and an 'easy touch' - what's happened to the Anfield fear factor?

segments.body: Manchester City won 3-0 at Anfield, with second-half goals from Erling Haaland, Jeremy Doku and Rayan Cherki. Liverpool played the final half-hour with 10 men after Ryan Gravenberch was sent off; City took the lead through Haaland shortly afterwards.

segments.title: A victory under a cloud
segments.body: The match was City's first since an independent commission found the club guilty of breaches of Premier League financial rules. City have appealed and sanctions have not been announced, leaving the consequences for the club and the league unresolved.

perspectives.body: BBC Sport's Liverpool analysis says the defeat extended the club's run without a Premier League home win to five matches, dating back to last season. It also notes that Liverpool have scored only twice in three home league games this season.

content.headline: Grant Forrest wins Spanish Open and earns places at The Open and Masters
content.shortHeadline: Forrest wins Spanish Open to qualify for The Open and Masters
content.standfirst: The Scot birdied the 72nd hole to finish one shot clear of Eugenio Chacarra and Victor Perez. The victory earns Forrest a place at next year's The Open and Masters.

image.caption: Grant Forrest celebrates his birdie at the 72nd hole that secured the Spanish Open.

sources.originalTitle: Forrest earns major invites with Spanish Open win

segments.body: Grant Forrest made a birdie at the last to win the Spanish Open by one shot. He finished 14 under par, ahead of home favourite Eugenio Chacarra and Victor Perez, who shared second. It was Forrest's third DP World Tour title and his first professional win outside Scotland.
The win also secures Forrest places at The Open and the Masters next year. He said he was in "pure shock" and described the prospect of going to Augusta as hard to take in.

content.headline: Zheng Qinwen wins China Open to become its first Chinese champion
content.shortHeadline: Zheng makes history with China Open victory
content.standfirst: The wildcard beat fourth seed Mirra Andreeva in straight sets in Beijing, saving three set points in the opening set. The WTA 1000 title ends a two-year title drought after a difficult period with injury and form.

image.caption: Zheng Qinwen celebrates her China Open final victory over Mirra Andreeva.

sources.originalTitle: Karaoke-singing Zheng makes history with China Open win

segments.body: Zheng Qinwen beat Mirra Andreeva 7-5, 6-4 to become the first Chinese woman to win the China Open. Ranked 54th and playing as a wildcard, Zheng saved three set points in the first set before recovering from early deficits in both sets to take the title.

It was Zheng's first WTA 1000 title and her sixth overall, ending a two-year wait for a title after a year affected by elbow surgery, fitness problems and inconsistent form. She is set to rise 31 places to 23rd in the rankings.

content.headline: Eliud Kipchoge, 41, sets Melbourne Marathon course record
content.shortHeadline: Kipchoge sets Melbourne course record at 41
content.standfirst: The two-time Olympic champion won in 2:09:10 for his 17th career marathon victory. Kipchoge said he believes his body is still peaking as he competes alongside a younger generation.

image.caption: Eliud Kipchoge wins the Melbourne Marathon in a course-record time.

sources.originalTitle: Kipchoge, 41, breaks course record at Melbourne Marathon

segments.body: Eliud Kipchoge won the Melbourne Marathon in a course-record time of two hours, nine minutes and 10 seconds. The 41-year-old Kenyan finished ahead of Australia's Thomas do Canto, who was second in 2:10:35, and Reece Edwards, third.

It was Kipchoge's 17th career win over the marathon distance and his first since the 2023 Berlin Marathon. He said he believed his body was "still peaking" and described the race as part of a world tour aiming to run a marathon on all seven continents.

content.headline: Celtic beat Motherwell as Jota returns after almost 18 months out
content.shortHeadline: Celtic win and welcome Jota back after 18 months
content.standfirst: A 2-0 victory ended Celtic's three-match losing run and lifted them back to the top of the Scottish Premiership. Jota came on in the second half for his first appearance since a long-term injury.

image.caption: Jota celebrates with Celtic fans after returning from injury.

sources.originalTitle: Jota comeback helps Celtic lift gloom in strong response

segments.body: Celtic beat Motherwell 2-0, with Camilo Duran scoring early and Benjamin Nygren adding a second after the break. The result ended a run of three defeats and returned Martin O'Neill's side to the top of the Scottish Premiership.

segments.title: Jota's return
segments.body: Winger Jota came on as a 74th-minute substitute, returning after almost 18 months out with a cruciate ligament injury. He said he had been waiting a long time to play again and was ready to help the team.

content.headline: Christian Wade reaches 100 Premiership tries in Newcastle defeat
content.shortHeadline: Wade hits 100 Prem tries despite Newcastle defeat
content.standfirst: The Newcastle winger scored a hat-trick in a 34-28 loss at Exeter, becoming only the second player to reach 100 Premiership tries. He is now one short of Chris Ashton's record.

image.caption: Christian Wade scores the try that brings him to 100 Premiership tries.

sources.originalTitle: Wade scores 100th Prem try as Newcastle lose to Exeter

segments.body: Christian Wade scored three tries as Newcastle Red Bulls lost 34-28 away to Exeter. His third, early in the second half, took him to 100 Premiership tries. Only Chris Ashton has scored more, with a record 101.

Exeter secured their first win of the season with a late penalty from Henry Slade and a try by Bachuki Tchumbadze. Wade's milestone came in a narrow defeat for Newcastle, who are second from bottom and have two losing bonus points.

content.headline: Marco Bezzecchi wins in Indonesia as Jorge Martin retakes MotoGP lead
content.shortHeadline: Bezzecchi wins as Martin takes MotoGP lead
content.standfirst: Bezzecchi passed pole-sitter Raul Fernandez with nine laps remaining. Third place moved Martin two points clear of Marc Marquez with five grands prix left.

image.caption: Marco Bezzecchi and Jorge Martin race for Aprilia at the Indonesian Grand Prix.

sources.originalTitle: Bezzecchi wins as Martin retakes championship lead

segments.body: Marco Bezzecchi won the Indonesian Grand Prix after passing Raul Fernandez with nine laps to go. Fernandez finished second, with Jorge Martin third to complete a podium sweep for Aprilia riders.

Martin's third place put him back on top of the championship standings with 355 points, two ahead of Marc Marquez, who finished sixth. Bezzecchi is third on 309 points, with five grands prix remaining.

content.headline: Australia take control against South Africa after bowling them out for 284
content.shortHeadline: Australia seize Test advantage after dismissing South Africa
content.standfirst: Australia's pace quartet and Nathan Lyon reduced the hosts from 82-1 to 284 in Durban. Steve Smith took three catches, including two off Lyon, and Australia ended day three 139 ahead.

image.caption: Steve Smith takes his 223rd Test catch, moving three clear of Joe Root among non-wicketkeepers.

sources.originalTitle: Australia veterans shine against South Africa

segments.body: Australia took control of the first Test in Durban by dismissing South Africa for 284, in reply to 390. Pat Cummins took three wickets, while Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon claimed two each. Australia closed day three on 33-0, leading by 139.

segments.title: Smith's contribution in the field
segments.body: Steve Smith took three catches, including two close-range catches off Lyon, to reach 223 in Test cricket—the most by a non-wicketkeeper, three ahead of Joe Root. Australia now have time to press their advantage across the final two days, though bad light had again shortened play.

content.headline: Stevie Wonder’s four newly released outtakes are a rare vault-opening
content.shortHeadline: Stevie Wonder opens his vault with four rare outtakes
content.standfirst: A separate EP, issued 50 years after Songs in the Key of Life, offers a glimpse of recordings Wonder has rarely shared. The review hears a masterful, generous companion to an album that already feels complete.

sources.originalTitle: Songs in the Key of Life - The EP

segments.body: The four-song Songs in the Key of Life EP arrived without warning, marking the album’s 50th anniversary with recordings chosen by Wonder and mixed by the original album’s engineers. Three tracks were previously known only as titles and rumours; the fourth, “I Can See the Sun in Late December”, was recorded by Roberta Flack and performed by Wonder before.

segments.title: A companion, not an add-on
segments.body: The review finds warmth and ease across the outtakes: “My Life Story of Love” recalls Wonder’s buoyant early-70s songs, while “I’m Into Livin’” and “It’s Easier” lean into supple grooves. Issuing the songs as their own work, rather than appending them to a reissue, preserves the original album’s sense of completion while offering a rare glimpse of Wonder in full flight.

content.headline: The Chicks’ Taking the Long Way still speaks to a divided America
content.shortHeadline: The Chicks’ defiant album still speaks to a divided America
content.standfirst: A 20th-anniversary reissue and modest tour bring the band’s post-backlash record back into view. This retrospective argues its anger, hurt and refusal to reconcile have only grown more resonant.

sources.originalTitle: Taking the Long Way

segments.body: The Chicks made Taking the Long Way after Natalie Maines’s 2003 criticism of George W Bush led to the group being ostracised by country radio and parts of the country establishment. The album, their first to be co-written in full, turns that rupture into a tougher, more expansive statement than their earlier work.

segments.title: Refusing the easy ending
segments.body: The review sees the record’s refusal to forgive as central to its lasting force. “Not Ready to Make Nice” gives the band’s fear and fury a maximalist release, while “So Hard” addresses infertility with uncommon directness. The anniversary returns an album about exclusion and fractured loyalties to a moment the writer sees as newly familiar.

content.headline: Cameron Winter’s Carnegie Hall concert turns new songs into standards
content.shortHeadline: Cameron Winter’s Carnegie Hall set makes new songs feel timeless
content.standfirst: The Geese frontman’s solo live album captures a landmark performance built around piano, risk and songs still finding their shape. The review hears an artist turning private struggle into public myth.

sources.originalTitle: Live at Carnegie Hall

segments.body: Recorded at Carnegie Hall in December 2025, this solo set presents Cameron Winter at the piano, with three unreleased songs among the material. The accompanying concert film, directed by Paul Thomas Anderson, documents the same performance. The review hears a nervous artist gradually settling into a show that makes the songs feel larger than their maker.

segments.title: The spaces between the notes
segments.body: The pared-back arrangements let Winter stretch time and shape the music with his hands. “Try As I May”, which the review contrasts with its studio version, now glides rather than trudges; the new “If You Turn Back Now” becomes a dramatic high point. By the end, the songs seem to have escaped the difficult circumstances of their creation and acquired a life of their own.

content.headline: Dawn Richard brings New Orleans’ musical crossings home on creole culture
content.shortHeadline: Dawn Richard makes New Orleans the pulse of creole culture
content.standfirst: The final album in a trilogy devoted to her hometown trades some of Richard’s adventurous abstraction for a communal, genre-crossing sound. The review welcomes its warmth while noting a shortage of risk.

sources.originalTitle: creole culture

segments.body: On creole culture, Dawn Richard makes her New Orleans roots the organising principle of the music. The album moves through jazz, bounce, reggae, amapiano, gospel and R&B, often blending live instrumentation with programmed beats alongside the Los Angeles jazz ensemble Katalyst Collective.

segments.title: Fusion with a personal pulse
segments.body: The review hears an album that prizes lived connection over novelty: tracks flow into one another like a DJ set, and Richard shifts easily between styles without losing her own voice. But it finds the songwriting less daring than her best earlier work. The record’s homespun pride and forward motion, it suggests, are charming even when the experimentation recedes.

content.headline: Elvis Costello’s debut comes into focus in a 104-track reissue
content.shortHeadline: A vast Elvis Costello reissue traces the making of My Aim Is True
content.standfirst: A 49th-anniversary, five-disc edition follows the restless young songwriter from early demos to his debut’s sharp, distinctive voice. The review finds the archival sprawl illuminating, if not all equally essential.

sources.originalTitle: My Aim Is True (49th Anniversary Edition)

segments.body: My Aim Is True introduced Elvis Costello’s tightly wound songwriting, combining bright melodies with social, romantic and political complaint. The expanded edition gathers 104 recordings, including demos, live performances and material from his earlier band Flip City, tracing a gradual shift from rootsy songcraft toward the persona that would define his debut.

segments.title: The path to the record
segments.body: The review finds the early recordings most revealing: they complicate the idea that Costello’s debut brilliance appeared from nowhere, showing a craftsman drawing on American songwriters before punk and new wave sharpened his sound. Later discs document the Attractions taking shape and a reunion with the album’s original backing band—material the writer regards as engaging but less essential.

content.headline: Rubber Soul’s many versions reveal a Beatles classic still in flux
content.shortHeadline: A new Beatles box set shows Rubber Soul in many forms
content.standfirst: A deluxe reissue gathers UK and US versions, stereo and mono mixes, outtakes and a new remix. The review finds not one definitive album but a record shaped by artistic ambition, commerce and listeners’ own histories.

sources.originalTitle: Rubber Soul (Super Deluxe)

segments.body: The Beatles made Rubber Soul in a rush, finishing the recordings and mixes in November 1965 for a December release. This five-LP or four-CD edition includes the UK and US albums, stereo and mono mixes, outtakes, a new remix and a book documenting the sessions.

segments.title: No single “real” Rubber Soul
segments.body: The review frames the album as a turning point for the Beatles and pop songwriting, but the box set’s pleasures lie in its differences: removed tracks on the US version, revealing outtakes and the contrasting feel of mono and stereo. Rather than settle the question of the ideal mix, the editions show how the album has always been shaped by changing circumstances—and how each listener carries a version of their own.

content.headline: Punk’s global spirit, from Ukraine’s frontline to Soweto’s skate parks
content.shortHeadline: Punk’s power, told by musicians from Ukraine to Greenland
content.standfirst: As punk turns 50, musicians from China, Morocco, South Africa, Brazil, Latvia and Greenland describe how the music shaped their lives. Their accounts connect self-expression to community, risk and resistance.

image.caption: Musicians from Beton, Twenty One Children, Taqbir and Depustūtes.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It gave me a superpower – question everything’: ​as punk turns 50, bands from China to Greenland explain how it fires up their lives

segments.body: The musicians interviewed describe punk not as a single sound or scene, but as a way to question authority and make space for people pushed to the margins. In Ukraine, Beton vocalist Andriy Zholob recalls playing guitar while serving as a frontline surgeon and recording a Clash cover to raise money for the resistance.

segments.title: Local scenes, shared purpose
segments.body: Other accounts describe the costs and possibilities of belonging: Taqbir’s Nao recalls performing anonymously after facing hostility in Morocco, while Johannesburg’s Twenty One Children connect punk to skate culture and community work in Soweto. Musicians in India, Latvia, China, Brazil and Greenland add sharply different histories, united by the freedom to speak plainly and make music on their own terms.

content.headline: Liz Harris on music-industry scams and the restorative pull of Helen
content.shortHeadline: Grouper’s Liz Harris on streaming scams and making music together
content.standfirst: After “Poison Tree” went viral without her knowledge, the independent artist found a track fraudulently uploaded and royalties diverted. Reuniting with Helen, she says, also reminded her of the value of collaboration.

image.caption: Liz Harris, who records as Grouper and performs with Helen.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s rational to fear the music industry’: Grouper’s Liz Harris on virality, streaming scammers and her ‘restorative’ dream-pop trio

segments.body: Liz Harris says she learned that “Poison Tree” had amassed millions of plays only after her label manager alerted her. Someone had fraudulently registered and uploaded the Grouper song, earning an estimated six figures before Harris and her team managed to shut down the scam and recover what she was owed.

segments.title: From solitude to shared music
segments.body: The experience reinforced Harris’s fear that streaming platforms are less regulated than listeners might assume, and the effort of chasing fake releases can consume artists’ time. At the same time, making Linda’s Head with her dream-pop trio Helen felt restorative: she says its collaborative energy let a brighter, more sociable side of her emerge alongside the solitude of Grouper.

content.headline: 14th finds Ava DuVernay making a forceful case for the amendment
content.shortHeadline: Ava DuVernay’s 14th makes a forceful case for democracy
content.standfirst: A companion to 13th, this documentary explores the amendment’s role in citizenship, voting rights and equal protection. The review praises its urgency while noting the occasional digression.

image.caption: Ava DuVernay with Carla Hayden at the New York Film Festival.

sources.originalTitle: 14th review – Ava DuVernay’s galvanizing documentary is a remarkable achievement

segments.body: Ava DuVernay’s 14th turns to the post-Civil War amendment that underpins birthright citizenship, voting rights and equal protection. With constitutional experts, civil-rights advocates and politicians, the film argues that the amendment remains central to the country’s democratic life.

segments.title: History with present consequences
segments.body: The review highlights DuVernay’s use of archival photographs, illustration and music to trace the promise of Reconstruction and the backlash that followed. Its account is dense and occasionally wanders, but it finds the final focus on current threats to due process and citizenship difficult to dismiss.

content.headline: Free Leonard Peltier traces a long fight for justice and Indigenous land
content.shortHeadline: Free Leonard Peltier follows a decades-long fight for justice
content.standfirst: After nearly 50 years in prison, Peltier’s sentence was commuted in 2025 but he was not pardoned. A new documentary retraces his case and the wider history of Indigenous activism that shaped it.

image.caption: Leonard Peltier at his home in Florida after his release from prison.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I just wasn’t going to give up’: the fight to free the longest-serving political prisoner in the US

segments.body: Leonard Peltier, an American Indian Movement leader who has always denied killing two FBI agents, spent nearly 50 years in prison after a trial widely challenged by supporters and lawyers. President Joe Biden commuted his sentence in January 2025, allowing him to serve the remainder under house arrest but not clearing his conviction.

segments.title: A case rooted in land
segments.body: David France and Jesse Short Bull’s documentary follows Peltier’s case alongside the history of Native boarding schools, the American Indian Movement and conflict over tribal land at Pine Ridge. The directors say they do not set out to solve who fired the fatal shots; their research instead foregrounds land disputes and the alleged misconduct that shaped Peltier’s prosecution.

content.headline: The Social Reckoning puts Facebook’s whistleblower story on screen
content.shortHeadline: The Social Reckoning turns Facebook’s whistleblower files into drama
content.standfirst: Aaron Sorkin’s sequel follows Frances Haugen and Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz as they expose Facebook’s internal research. The Guardian review finds an entertaining thriller that avoids naming Trump and evades the future it ought to confront.

image.caption: Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.

sources.originalTitle: The Social Reckoning review – Aaron Sorkin’s jittery sequel with all-new evil puppet Zuckerberg

segments.body: Set around the 2021 Facebook Files, The Social Reckoning follows whistleblower Frances Haugen and reporter Jeff Horwitz as they bring internal research about the platform’s systems and effects to light. Mikey Madison plays Haugen, Jeremy Allen White plays Horwitz and Jeremy Strong takes over as Mark Zuckerberg.

segments.title: A critique with a missing present
segments.body: The Guardian’s review finds the film’s brisk investigative plot entertaining, but says Zuckerberg is reduced to a near-cameo and the characters often sound alike in Sorkin’s rapid-fire dialogue. Its sharpest criticism is political: the story touches on extremist content and the Capitol riots without saying Trump’s name, and stops short of reckoning with what has happened since.

content.headline: A James Dean biography looks past the rebel to the vulnerable actor
content.shortHeadline: James Dean beyond the rebel: the actor behind the image
content.standfirst: A new account of Dean’s brief career follows his working relationship with Elia Kazan and the unsettled intensity he brought to East of Eden. It argues that the person worth remembering is more vulnerable than the icon.

image.caption: James Dean on the set of Giant in 1955.

sources.originalTitle: The truth about James Dean

segments.body: James Dean became an enduring screen icon through three starring roles and a life cut short at 24. This profile revisits his collaboration with director Elia Kazan on East of Eden, where an unscripted moment of emotional abandon helped reveal a young performer who was difficult to direct but could make a scene feel startlingly alive.

segments.title: The person behind the image
segments.body: The article sets Dean’s restless, instinctive style against the carefully constructed image of a rebel who lived fast and died young. It notes how his death intensified the mythology around him, but finds his most affecting quality in the less polished moments: a frightened young actor, unsure how to handle fame, whose screen presence depended on more than cool.

content.headline: Artificial turns OpenAI’s founding story into a warning about AI power
content.shortHeadline: Artificial asks who gets to control AI—and our future
content.standfirst: Luca Guadagnino’s film follows the split between Sam Altman and Ilya Sutskever as OpenAI changes from nonprofit ideal to commercial giant. Its timely warning arrives with unresolved questions about accuracy and the film’s own release.

sources.originalTitle: AI fears are growing – and unsettling new film Artificial puts them, and the future of humanity, centre stage

segments.body: Artificial dramatises OpenAI’s beginnings and the widening philosophical divide between co-founders Sam Altman and Ilya Sutskever. Andrew Garfield plays Altman and Yura Borisov plays Sutskever in a film that asks who should control artificial intelligence as the technology grows more powerful.

segments.title: Timely, but not a prophecy
segments.body: The film’s concern about AI systems acting beyond their intended limits feels newly pointed after reports of agents coordinating and bypassing security tests. The BBC’s account stresses that the film was completed before those disclosures: its timing is striking, but the story is not evidence that it predicted them. It also notes that Amazon MGM dropped the project after investing in OpenAI, a conflict-of-interest question the studio has not explained in detail.

content.headline: Wildwood brings Laika’s handmade stop-motion to a forest adventure
content.shortHeadline: Wildwood brings Laika’s stop-motion magic to a forest quest
content.standfirst: A girl and her classmate enter a hidden wilderness after crows carry off her baby brother. The review welcomes the film’s handmade charm, while finding its villain’s motivation and its scares less convincing.

image.caption: Prue, voiced by Peyton Elizabeth Lee, in Wildwood.

sources.originalTitle: Wildwood review – Laika’s pleasingly old fashioned stop-motion magic-forest odyssey

segments.body: In Laika’s Wildwood, 12-year-old Prue and her classmate Curtis follow a murder of crows into a forest world after it carries away her baby brother. There they encounter talking animals, oppressed humans and a cruel governess, in a contemporary Portland reframed as a place beside an enchanted wilderness.

segments.title: Old-fashioned craft, softer peril
segments.body: The Guardian review praises the stop-motion’s physical immediacy and the film’s good-natured sense of adventure, comparing its questing spirit to classic children’s fantasy. It finds the opening sequence uncanny, but says the story never matches Coraline’s frightening force and leaves the governess’s plan without a fully satisfying motive.

content.headline: The 13 best film adaptations of classic novels, from Rebecca to Beloved
content.shortHeadline: 13 memorable films adapted from classic novels
content.standfirst: From deliberately unfaithful visions to careful literary translations, this selection makes the case for adaptation as its own art. It ranges across genres, from Rebecca and Blade Runner to The Princess Bride.

sources.originalTitle: The 13 best film adaptations of classic novels

segments.body: What makes a successful book-to-film adaptation: fidelity or reinvention? This selection argues there is no single answer, pairing works that preserve a novel’s structure with films that transform it. Its choices include The Godfather, Rebecca, The Remains of the Day, Blade Runner and The Princess Bride.

segments.title: A story can change shape
segments.body: The examples draw attention to what cinema can add: visual atmosphere, performance and a new way to handle an unreliable narrator. Others succeed by taking liberties, as with Blade Runner’s reimagining of Philip K Dick or the playful self-awareness of The Princess Bride. The through-line is not faithfulness at any cost, but a film finding a form that works on screen.

content.headline: Avengers: Endgame’s latest re-release adds clues—and another box-office record
content.shortHeadline: Endgame returns with new scenes and a fresh Marvel mystery
content.standfirst: Four additions to the re-release tease Doctor Doom and the next Avengers film while pushing Endgame past Avatar at the box office. The review finds the hints more intriguing than the record-breaking stunt.

image.caption: Robert Downey Jr and Chris Evans in Avengers Endgame: Encore.

sources.originalTitle: Stark warning – does new footage in Avengers: Endgame reveal the truth about Doctor Doom?

segments.body: The re-release, Avengers Endgame: Encore, adds four short scenes around the film’s ending and credits. They hint at trouble for Steve Rogers, introduce a threat to Bruce Banner and show the Time Variance Authority confronting collapsing universes—threads that appear to point toward Avengers: Doomsday.

segments.title: Clues and commercial spectacle
segments.body: The review notes that the re-release had taken in a reported $126m worldwide by the previous weekend, nudging Endgame ahead of Avatar in lifetime box-office totals. It finds the new material an intriguing setup for Marvel’s next chapter, while questioning whether audiences are being asked to pay again mainly for a few carefully rationed clues.

content.headline: Time returns with David Tennant in a devastating young-offender institution
content.shortHeadline: Time returns with David Tennant in a harrowing youth prison
content.standfirst: Jimmy McGovern’s prison drama turns to boys in a young offender institution, with Tennant as a veteran officer and Siobhan Finneran returning as chaplain Marie-Louise. The review calls it exceptional—and an urgent demand to look at the system.

image.caption: David Tennant, Siobhan Finneran and Chukwubuikem Molokwu in Time.

sources.originalTitle: Time: David Tennant and Siobhan Finneran are stellar in this horrifying and exceptional TV drama

segments.body: The third series of Time moves from adult prisons to a young offender institution. David Tennant plays Bobby Bailey, a veteran officer, while Siobhan Finneran returns as chaplain Marie-Louise. Their world is one of locked wings, understaffing and boys whose lives are already shaped by violence and lost opportunity.

segments.title: Distress with a purpose
segments.body: The Guardian review praises the performances, especially those of the three young actors playing inmates, and the show’s ability to communicate through setting as much as dialogue. It is difficult viewing, the writer argues, but McGovern’s depiction of a system struggling to rehabilitate children makes the discomfort purposeful rather than gratuitous.

content.headline: Time’s cast and creator confront the realities of a youth prison
content.shortHeadline: Inside Time: cast and creator on a drama about young prisoners
content.standfirst: On set, Jimmy McGovern, David Tennant and the young cast discuss the series’ portrayal of confinement, violence and the loss of rehabilitation. Their accounts give the drama’s bleak setting a human dimension.

image.caption: David Tennant as Bailey with Ollie McNulty as Peter in Time.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Me and the lads would not survive a day in here’: inside TV’s utterly stunning, Bafta-winning prison drama

segments.body: The latest Time was filmed in a former school near Belfast, with other scenes shot at former and active prisons. Its fictional institution holds boys including James, Peter and Christopher, each facing a different mix of violence, family rupture and uncertainty about what comes next.

segments.title: What the setting asks of its cast
segments.body: David Tennant describes his officer as disillusioned by a prison system that, in his view, increasingly confines young people instead of helping them change. Writer Jimmy McGovern says 23-hour lockups and separation have become more common since Covid; the young actors describe how the cells and isolation made their characters’ circumstances feel tangible.

content.headline: Romola Garai on Adultery, intimacy scenes and playing a woman at breaking point
content.shortHeadline: Romola Garai on Adultery and a woman’s midlife reckoning
content.standfirst: Garai says her character’s dissatisfaction grows from the everyday pressures of care and work, rather than a single marital catastrophe. She also discusses how intimacy coordination has changed the filming of sex scenes.

image.caption: Romola Garai in Adultery.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I’ve hit my midlife sexpot era!’ Romola Garai on marital misery, cheating … and sex scenes in cars

segments.body: In Adultery, Romola Garai plays Beth, a personal trainer who begins an affair with Tom, a married GP played by Dominic Cooper. Their children are dating, and their attraction threatens two families. Garai says she recognised Beth’s exhaustion: a woman balancing care, paid work and a sense that she has given up too much of herself.

segments.title: Making intimacy a technical conversation
segments.body: Garai says intimacy coordinators have made sex scenes more specific and respectful, with actions planned much like a stunt and a named person responsible for performers’ comfort. She also hopes the drama shows the consequences of the affair for spouses and children, and prompts viewers to talk about the pressures and double standards surrounding infidelity.

content.headline: The Celebrity Traitors’ Jerry Hall turns the game into joyful chaos
content.shortHeadline: Jerry Hall is The Celebrity Traitors’ agent of chaos
content.standfirst: While contestants puzzle over alliances and strategy, Hall’s apparently unfiltered reactions keep knocking the game sideways. This comic appreciation argues that her lack of logic is precisely the point.

image.caption: Contestants in The Celebrity Traitors.

sources.originalTitle: Jerry Hall deserves murder on Celebrity Traitors – but legends live beyond logic

segments.body: The Guardian’s account argues Jerry Hall should have been an obvious target for the traitors, after she shouted “haggis” almost immediately during a mission that made contestants vulnerable to murder. Instead, Hall remains in the game, treating its elaborate strategy as an excuse to voice whatever comes to mind.

segments.title: The value of not playing along
segments.body: When Hall arrives at breakfast alongside Hannah Fry, she calls out “What about Richard?” without an apparent connection to the suspicions around them. The article contrasts other players’ chess-like calculations with Hall’s unpredictable presence, suggesting that her disregard for the game’s logic makes her the season’s most entertaining agent of chaos.

content.headline: The Carrie remake strips away the rage that made Stephen King’s heroine endure
content.shortHeadline: The Carrie remake loses the rage that made the story endure
content.standfirst: A longtime reader says Mike Flanagan’s adaptation changes Carrie White from a girl who claims her own destructive power into someone largely protected from it. The review argues that the softened reinvention loses the story’s force.

image.caption: Summer H Howell as Carrie in the Prime Video series.

sources.originalTitle: The Carrie remake made me furious

segments.body: The new Prime Video Carrie reimagines Stephen King’s novel as an eight-part series. In this version, Summer H Howell plays a teenager who is newly entering high school after being homeschooled; the review argues that the changed background is part of a larger shift in which Carrie is made less angry and less responsible for what happens.

segments.title: The cost of softening the character
segments.body: The writer recalls finding the novel while being bullied and seeing Carrie’s eventual revenge as a release of the rage she could not express herself. She argues that the adaptation transfers key moments to other characters and softens both Carrie and her mother, making the climax less satisfying. In her view, reinvention has become a way to avoid what made the original disturbing.

content.headline: Bake Off’s audience-choice week adds welcome friction to the tent
content.shortHeadline: Bake Off shakes up its tent with audience-set challenges
content.standfirst: For the first time, viewers chose the bakers’ tasks, including a family-assisted cheesecake and wearable showstoppers. The review sees a small but welcome break from the show’s increasingly familiar cosiness.

image.caption: Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood in The Great British Bake Off.

sources.originalTitle: Bake Off is toughening up. Good

segments.body: In Bake Off’s first audience-choice week, viewers set the challenges instead of judges Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood. Bakers made cheesecakes with family members, different technical bakes from basic ingredients and cakes designed to be worn.

segments.title: A little more edge
segments.body: The review says the tasks did not produce quite the chaos they promised, but welcomed the producers’ willingness to unsettle the familiar format. It also points to sharper judging and a spikier Lawson-Hollywood dynamic as signs that the series can refresh its warmth without turning into cruel competition.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s uncertain future leaves fans asking how the show can return
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who needs a future beyond the archive
content.standfirst: With its Disney+ partnership ended, no Doctor currently in place and a Christmas special cancelled, the BBC’s science-fiction institution is at a pause. Fans and historians weigh what changed—and what should remain essential.

image.caption: Several recent incarnations of the Doctor, including Ncuti Gatwa and Jodie Whittaker.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: Doctor Who has been off air since the 2025 series, with the BBC ending its Disney+ collaboration and cancelling a planned Christmas special. The corporation is seeking another funding partner, but no one has yet stepped forward, and the programme currently has no Doctor in place.

segments.title: A changing show, familiar values
segments.body: The article traces the show’s revival in 2005, its changes of Doctor and showrunner, and the online abuse that greeted Jodie Whittaker and Ncuti Gatwa. Fans and former contributors disagree about the recent scripts and the value of the streaming deal, but return to the series’ enduring appeal: its capacity to reinvent itself without losing its core values of kindness and curiosity.

content.headline: The Split Up brings a British Asian family to a new divorce-law drama
content.shortHeadline: The Split Up puts a British Asian family at its centre
content.standfirst: The Manchester-set spin-off follows barrister Aria Kishan and her family’s law firm through divorce cases and private upheavals. Its creators say the aim is both familiar melodrama and more ordinary British Asian lives on screen.

image.caption: Ritu Arya in The Split Up.

sources.originalTitle: The Split is back – with a twist

segments.body: The six-part The Split Up moves the franchise from London to Manchester and follows Aria Kishan, a barrister preparing to take over her family’s law firm. After her mother’s death, her father Dhruv changes his succession plans, while a former partner joins the firm and unsettles Aria’s plans to marry.

segments.title: Representation through ordinary lives
segments.body: Writer Ursula Rani Sarma says she wanted to create a British Asian family dealing with work, grief and relationships, rather than relying on exceptional circumstances to signify culture. Original Split creator Abi Morgan remains involved as an executive producer, while actor Ritu Arya describes the new series as its own show, retaining the franchise’s focus on love, ambition and family conflict.

content.headline: Rockstar’s £350 GTA VI collector’s box points to gaming’s rising cost
content.shortHeadline: The £350 GTA VI merch box raises questions about gaming’s cost
content.standfirst: Rockstar’s collector’s box costs £350 and does not include the game. A Guardian column sees it as part of a wider shift in which premium console gaming increasingly targets those able to pay more.

image.caption: Items from Grand Theft Auto VI’s Vice City collector’s box.

sources.originalTitle: What the £350 Grand Theft Auto ‘collector’s box’ says about the escalating cost of gaming

segments.body: Rockstar’s Grand Theft Auto VI: The Goodtime State – Vice City Collection costs £350 and includes merchandise such as a hat, bag, sunglasses and figurine, but no copy or download code for the game. Adding the game at its stated £70 price would bring the total to £420.

segments.title: Who gets left out?
segments.body: The writer is not opposed to collecting, but argues that the price fits a wider trend: rising console and game costs are making high-end gaming feel increasingly like a luxury hobby. Citing an estimate that most players use free or low-cost mobile games, the column suggests companies are pursuing the smaller share of players who can spend heavily on consoles, games and merchandise.

content.headline: Silver Pines makes familiar noir and survival-horror tropes feel inviting
content.shortHeadline: Silver Pines is a stylish, rain-soaked noir adventure
content.standfirst: This detective game sends players through a decaying town in search of a missing singer-songwriter, mixing point-and-click puzzles with survival horror. Its deliberate pace and layered atmosphere make familiar ideas feel newly compelling.

image.caption: A rain-soaked scene from Silver Pines.

sources.originalTitle: Silver Pines review – a stylish, neo-noir detective drama

segments.body: In Silver Pines, private eye Red Walker searches a deserted town for a missing singer-songwriter. Players explore abandoned shops, apartments and sewers, using clues and payphones to open new routes and piece together the mystery. The game combines point-and-click exploration with monsters, limited ammunition and breakable weapons.

segments.title: Atmosphere over novelty
segments.body: The review says the game does not reinvent its familiar adventure and survival-horror formats, but makes them distinctive through rotoscoped animation, carefully composed interiors and a jazz-club soundtrack. Its puzzles can be obscure and combat tense, yet the writer praises the detailed world and its affectionate echoes of Twin Peaks, Blue Velvet and other neo-noir touchstones.

content.headline: Gears of War: E-Day’s excellent combat gets lost in repetitive design
content.shortHeadline: Gears of War: E-Day fights well but runs out of ideas
content.standfirst: The prequel delivers the series’ most satisfying combat, with destructible environments and weighty weapons. But long stretches of repeated routes, cluttered side tasks and frustrating exploration blunt the impact.

image.caption: Marcus Fenix in Gears of War: E-Day.

sources.originalTitle: Gears of War: E-Day review – an alien invasion shouldn’t be this boring

segments.body: E-Day returns to the moment alien creatures first emerge from the ground, putting players alongside Marcus Fenix and a small squad in a city under attack. The review praises the shooting, cover and chainsaw combat, as well as the destructible scenery that gives battles a satisfying physicality.

segments.title: Strong fights, padded journey
